The school bell rings, and everyone in my class roars with excitement, and rushes out the door. I wait for everyone to walk out, so I can say bye to the teacher. "Bye miss!" I call out, and she responds with, "Bye Ellie!" I walk to the dragon stables, where I grab Mismatch, my pet dragon. I pat Mismatch, feeling her purple and blue scaly skin. She roars gently, bouncing a little, and I sense she is excited to go home.  I jump on her back, and we ride out of the school gates. Mismatch always makes me happy, but today I'm feeling excited, because my birthday is in two days! The wind is rushing through my hair, and grass is a blur we're going so fast. Suddenly, there's a loud thud! Mismatch roars, and suddenly halts to the ground. "Whoa, Mismatch, easy!" I murmur into her ear. She groans and rolls her head around. I take a look at her head, and there's a little red dent on her head. I vigorously turn my head, to see the possible things that could have hit Mismatch. There's crashed glass on the ground I see, and in the middle is a little scroll. It's a dark blue scratchy piece of paper, with small writing on it. I hop down to pick it up, and as I'm picking it up, a piece of glass cuts me deeply. "Ow!" I holler, looking down at my bleeding hand. I feel worried, yet curious at the same time. I pick up the scroll, and quickly scan it with my eyes. My eyes widen every word I read. It says,
You've started reading this, you can't escape it, so do what I say, or your doom will be near. Go to the grave yard, twelve o'clock at night sharp, meet me at the first grave, come alone, or else. 

I don't know what to do, I feel faint. Should I get help, or should I go? I've decided, I will go to the graveyard, at twelve o'clock, and I'll prove I'm no chicken!

Back at home, in my bedroom, I wonder what I should pack. My bag lies empty, stuff scattered over my bed. I'm contemplating torch, rope, food, or bubblegum. I'll bring it all I decide, well, maybe not the bubblegum, it isn't as necessary as everything else. I stuff it all into my small, old and rusty satchel , prepared for whatever is thrown at me. 

I still need to somehow convince mum and dad to somehow let me go. I don't think I can tell them where I'm going, because they will most definitely flip out if I tell them where I'm going. Maybe I'll say I'm going to a sleepover at Olivias house, or a study group. Well, a study group at twelve pm would be a little worrying,  so I'll just say I'm going for a sleepover. 

I bound downstairs, where I find mum and dad having a cup of coffee together. "Hey! Can I go to Olivias tonight for a sleepover?” I say a little too fast. “For study,” I say quickly, so they don’t get suspicious. “Sure kiddo,” dad replies smiling, “want me to drop you off?” 
“No, I can walk,” I say hurriedly, then I race upstairs. 

It’s time, it’s time for me to go and face my fears. I grab my satchel, and race out the door, feeling intimidated, but excited. I was contemplating whether to bring Mismatch, or keep her here. I decide to keep her here, because I don’t want her to get hurt. The air is cold, and I shiver, but keep on walking. I check the time on my watch, it’s eleven fifty, so I’m just on time. I approach the graveyard, it’s high iron fences towering over me, but I walk through. Something shrieks  in the distance, probably a bat, but I walk on through. 

There a wooden bench, and I sit down on it, wondering if this person is even going to show up. I check my watch again, and it’s twelve exactly. I look around, and I here some giggles, and shushes, and I feel petrified, when suddenly, “Surprise!”
Loads of people jump up, and come over and jump on me! “Huh?” I say.
“We wanted to plan you a surprise party, for you birthday of course!” Olivia says,
“Really? Thank you!” I say, and look around. There’s ballon’s, streamers, lights, food and most importantly, there a massive cake in the middle of the food table, reading, Happy Birthday Ellie!
“Thank you!” I yell to everyone, and I jump up and down from excitement.

creations.write_up:
Time and hands 

Lilli and her Dad sat on the rusty old bench, as they had since their beloved mum and wife had been gone.
“Dad?” Lilli asked. Before he could answer, she blurted out the question that had been on her mind since—well, ever since the accident. “Why do bad things happen?”
Dad seemed to hesitate, so Lilli held her breath, hoping he would answer.
“Well, I guess bad things happen so we know how important it is to savour every single moment we have,” Dad slowly answered to his daughter. “We need to know that something could happen at any time, so we need to appreciate each and every moment.”
Lilli squeezed her eyes shut, trying to push her dad’s words into her mind like a secret she never wanted to forget. 
“Okay...” Lilli answered through gritted teeth. 
“Lilli?”
“Yes, Dad?”
“I think the reason is that we need to appreciate everything in life, because anything is possible at any time. Time holds the secrets to the universe, and it’s what connects our past to the future. So through time, you are never alone, because you’ll always be connected to what’s been, and what’s yet to come.”
Lilli mumbled, “ So me and mum are like a string of thread  held together?”
Dad smiled, “Exactly.”
Lilli held her head up high, and said through a confident voice, “Dad, I’m going to look after my time. Because through time, I have my family, friends, and my surroundings—and I feel like that’s what matters to me.” Lilli took her time saying this.
Dad bit his lip and looked up at the fiery red setting sun. “I think you’re right. Time is everything.”

creations.write_up:
Little red riding hood: the truth 

Cruelty is a curse, the more you commit, the more it becomes a habit; horrible and almost incurable.  And then you wonder, why? You could have spared yourself from the guilt, but you didn’t. You could have left the idea to linger quietly, burrowing deep into your mind. But you chose not to. And then you say: it’s just a small thing, right? To try to convince yourself that it will get better—but it won’t. Then you make an enemy, the victim, their hurt turns into fury. And the only one to blame is you. This tale is the same, an endless cycle of guilt and hatred. Little Red Riding Hood and her family stand as the killers of wolves for pleasure. The wolf lived in the fiction created by the world. The trees’ leaves shivered, as if every fallen paw made them recoil in disgust.
Did you ever wonder why her hood was red?

“Lupo!” The howl of his mother’s voice—beckoning him for dinner—echoed through the forest. Everything was quiet. Then her loud, impatient call shattered it, like a mirror breaking. Lupo sighed quietly. For if he wasn’t careful enough he would be punished by a lecture about ‘how being out in the woods is dangerous.’ He closed his eyes and took in the sound of leaves crinkling beneath his paws, the birds’ soft, melodic chirping through the canopy of leaves and branches, and the warmth of the sun beneath his fur. Just one more second. He thought. Lupo revelled in pretending; he would slip into the skin of someone else and watch his worries melt away as he submerged himself in the fantasy. He had pretended to be everything he could think of except humans. The filthy creatures robbed him of his father. But what if it was only that family? What if everyone else just believed in the easiest lie? They say life is a dream…but what if this one is a nightmare?

Your subconscious notices far more than your conscious mind ever could. Shadows lurk everywhere, waiting to strike; the worries your mind pushes away. The sound in the silence beckons you to a fake world. Lupo froze, his claws digging into the ground. Another shadow? He thought. Empty promises—never spoken, yet always obeyed—can poison minds as easily as a leaf falling from a tree. The puppeteers pull the world on the string fate weaves. Each animal or plant in the forest is made for one purpose. To feed their hunger. To satisfy their need for something to happen. All of this we sense, but don’t see. These chains bind us. Invisible, yet everyone can see them. If they look closer. Not with their eyes, but with their minds. With the sixth sense everyone has, but rarely perceives. If the wolf dies but no one’s around, who’s to tell the story?

Lupo crept out of the small, hidden den. This is my home, but what if I want a home somewhere else—the forest? What if my family isn’t the wolves I live with, but the nature surrounding me? His ears twitched and he abruptly stopped at every small sound he heard. As he came closer to the end of his village he saw the thorny gate made of twigs. It’s open. Lupo thought, excitement creeping in. His paws pressed against the lush ground and he felt the sunlight warm against his back. I’m free. 

Wolves kill. Humans watch, saddened by the loss of their loved ones, but dare not intervene. Lupo, the wolf. The killer. Little Red Riding Hood, the victim. The innocent child who befalls a terrible fate. The humans were right in some way. Wolves did kill…well, most of them. Everyone says wolves are disgusting, bloodshed and violence are the only things that satisfy us. The truth is we are forced into killing, humans are no different. We have to fight for our food. If they didn’t have luxuries they see as necessities, they would be like us too. We didn’t choose this. Humans chose it for us.

Lupo's ears twitched, the sound of a predator. He thought. The sun always shone, another element to the fiction created to deceive everyone. He sunk to the ground, feeling the grass brush against his face. Lupo crept towards the noise, each step as silent as secrets kept. He could hear his heart pounding through his ears, the noise overwhelmed him. What if…it’s a human. What if it’s them. He drew himself closer, step after step. Lupo froze. A child. A girl skipping along the dirt road. Happily singing, her red hood blowing in the breeze.

 No… he thought. I have to warn my family. But his body wouldn’t move. The cruel smirk that hid behind that innocent smile was almost unnoticeable. But Lupo could see it. That glint of evil. Hidden behind a mask created by thousands of lies. His ears flattened, and his fear forced a whimper. Little Red Riding Hood stopped dead in her tracks. Hand clasping the handle of the basket. Her expression immediately changed. She tilted her head in an unnatural way. Each step was meaningful. Lupo tensed and crouched lower to the floor. He could just see her shoes, black, polished boots. But there was something off. Lupo drew a sharp breath. Blood. On the heel. “Hey, wolf! You can come out! I’m not going to hurt you!” Her smile didn’t quite reach her eyes. “Here, you can have one of my pastries!” She reached into the basket. A small hand that could do so much damage. She threw a donut onto the floor, too forcefully to be innocent. “Don’t make me do this the hard way.” Lupo sniffed the pastry. Poison.

 Little Red Riding Hood reached into her pocket. She drew a knife, its tip stained with the blood of her fallen enemies. The knife glinted in the warm sunlight, a symbol of evidence. Her innocent demeanour lingered in the air, yet her grin conveyed something much darker. Lupo stepped away. The crunch of a leaf beneath his paw. Her smirk widened as she turned to face him. Lupo whimpered and ran. For the first time the forest seemed deadly. He crouched behind a tree, stiffening his whole body. “This could be easy, you're only denying the inevitable.” Little Red Riding Hood’s call rang through the forest. “Where are you?” Each step she took made the woods go silent. The thought of every victim sickened Lupo to his core. He felt bile rise in his throat while he forced back bitter tears. How did this happen? Maybe mother was right, the woods are dangerous. The world spun and Lupo found himself falling to the ground. He heard soft steps and a figure in red approaching. I never thought I’d die this way. Lupo smelled a faint aroma wafting from Little Red Riding Hood. Where have I smelled that before? Where the healers work back at home. Sleep’s blissful embrace wrapped around him, and the world faded into black. 

Her eyes flickered from side to side, satisfied that no one could see her—shrouded in a blanket of lies. Her strides were purposeful, each step towards the wolf made her heart pound faster. Even after years it still shook her. Does that mean I still care? The thought brought up memories she tried to push down. Her body shook as she pulled her hood over her head, concealing her face in a shadow. Bring the poison to your grandmother, make her eat it, kill any wolves you see. Her parents' words swam in her head. She brought the knife up, tightening her grip. She sighed. And then there was a rustle of leaves. 

Ruby immediately picked up her basket, stuffed the knife in her pocket and turned to face the noise. The lumberjack. Tall and broad, he stood proudly. He’s so arrogant, he has no idea how gullible he is. It was these moments that made her feel in control, she could manipulate anyone to believe her. And that’s what made her feel safe. Being able to create a world she could bend to her will. She smiled sweetly, “Lumberjack! What are you doing up at this hour? I thought you were too lazy to get out of bed.” "Well today I thought I would be productive.” He chuckled. Will he just go away? “Good for you, well you better get to chopping wood.” Little Red Riding Hood struggled to maintain the smile on her face. “See you later.” He briskly walked off into the forest.

As soon as the lumberjack was out of sight, Little Red Riding Hood's smile dropped. She shuddered as she drew the knife, paranoid of what it could do to her, if she did something wrong. If they found out she did. So she wouldn't, she promised herself she would stay out of harm's way and pretend. Not like acting—like concealing and deceiving others for so long you believe it yourself. You stop questioning the cycle of cruelty; you consider yourself lucky for not being the prey. But you're always the prey. Someone will always take control, and we let them. The heroes we know are never really true. It’s the people who quietly observe, they wait for the right time to strike. Like…the wolves.

Little Red Riding Hood. Does anyone actually know my name? Do my parents? Do they know my age? Probably not. They’re killers, nothing else. That’s all they’ve ever been. I was naive to think they’d accept me if I played along. She realised how long she had been staring at nothing. She turned around to face the wolf. It had woken up. “Excuse me but you have been staring at that knife for an awfully long time.” There was no hint of fear in its voice.

 “You can talk?” Little Red Riding Hood stepped back. “You didn’t know? Well anyway I’m Lupo. And you’re Little Red Riding Hood?” She calculated her response carefully. “Yeah…you aren’t scared of me?” “Yes I am to be honest. But I’ve been acting for so long I’m pretty much a professional.” I know what you’re trying to do. “Sometimes it’s nice to slip away to your own world. But at the same time it gets exhausting over time. Constantly pretending to be someone you’re not.” 

Little Red Riding Hood’s gaze softened slightly. Maybe he’s right. It is tiring. “Good point.” She shuffled uncomfortably at the thought. “I’ve never done anything to disobey my parents…I was taught to. But what if they deserve it, does that make it right?” “In my opinion, yes.” Lupo loosened his muscles and took a step towards Little Red Riding Hood. “Can I ask you something? Why didn’t you kill me?” “Huh?” “Why didn’t you kill me? You could’ve stopped me talking as easily as a bird spreading its wings. But you listened, and you waited. That shows you can be who you want. You just have to accept that some people are horrible.” She felt tears prick her eyes and she turned around. “I-i think it’s cruel how they kill wolves. I’ve never said it out loud but…” “Then come with me! You don’t have to obey them.” Little Red Riding Hood processed this. The weight of letting go. “The lie hurts more than the truth. I’ll come.”

They walked through the forest, along the winding dirt path. Lupo walked with excitement, Little Red Riding Hood, however, slowly dragged herself along, still petrified of what she had done. Twigs and leaves crunched beneath her boots. The red hood, a symbol of her connection to her parents, weighed her down. How did I let myself give in? No—I didn’t give in, I realised the truth. “Where are we going?” Little Red Riding Hood said in an attempt to stifle her thoughts. “Your grandma's house.” Lupo said casually, paws padding against the ground. “How do you know where that is?” “I watched you to see where not to go.” He’s smarter than I thought, maybe wolves aren’t stupid after all. A cottage slowly emerged from the distance. Colourful and bright compared to her past. The door creaked open. An old lady with graying hair, glasses and wrinkles stepped out. “Ruby! What are you doing here!” The old lady’s face was etched with excitement. She remembered my name—she’s the only one who did. “You haven’t visited me since…that day.” The joyful smile slid off her face with the mention of that day, Little Red Hiding Hood knew why; it was grandma's birthday…

Ruby felt the pounding in her ears as she carried the cake, its sweet smell wafting
through the air. “Are you excited to surprise grandma Little Red Riding Hood?” her mother stood beside her, a warm smile masking her cruelty. But Ruby didn’t know that. “Yeah! But why does she live in the middle of nowhere? I keep getting bitten by bugs.” “We're almost there.”  her father stood on the other side of her. Everything felt too…cohesive, like everything was planned. but ruby didn't notice, she was too caught up in the web of lies, and the idea she could weave her own. The cottage looked the same as it always did, bright and colourful. contrasting with the earthy tones of the surrounding forest. Ruby was five, and on her birthday had been given that red hood. She wore it on her grandma's birthday. Her grandma's face had immediately once she saw that red hood. Ruby's mother had given her a sharp look, her hand lingered near her pocket. where the knife was. “Can I talk to Ruby for a second? on her own.” It sounded more like an order than a question. Ruby's parents looked confused, then their eyes widened. They had forgotten my name and I didn't even notice. “I guess that's fine.” Ruby's mother responded hesitantly.

 Ruby remembered walking into the house, it smelt of perfume, bread and flowers. She had been there so many times but never noticed her parents shallow breathing whenever she did. They had sat her down and made her speak of anything she had heard. Grandma ushered her into a room. “There is something important I’ve been needing to tell you, but you must promise to never tell your parents and never speak a word of it.” “Okay, but only if I can have a donut first.” Grandma let out a laugh, heartfelt yet shaky. “Of course.” She opened the fridge and pulled out a caramel donut. “Thanks, your donuts are always the best. You should enter a contest.” Grandma’s expression darkened at the thought of going out on her own. “Now back to what I’m here to talk to you about. Your parents…are…killers. They murder wolves and turn people against them. Because of course no one bothers to figure out the truth.” “Why would they do that? It-it doesn’t make sense. How do I know you’re not lying?” She knew deep down grandma would never lie, but the thought of her own parents being so cruel was too unbearable. “I knew this would happen.” Grandma sighed and abruptly stood up and walked towards the basement. Ruby could feel the tension hanging in the air, suffocating her in the words she uttered.

Grandma strode back to the room and pulled out a chair. She held a small chest. “I didn’t want you to find out this early, but seeing as they gave you that hood…’ she trailed off. Ruby pulled the hood over her eyes. Grandma pulled out a rusted key. Holding it like an instrument in her wrinkled hands. Ruby’s chest tightened. The key clicked into place, a sound that filled the room with anticipation and fear. Grandma pulled out a stack of old, crumpled paper. Why does she have a bunch of crumpled newspapers? Maybe she’s just old and crazy. Whatever she tells me is probably twisted.

 “Your parents…kill wolves for no good cause.” Grandma reluctantly said. “But maybe there’s a good reason!” “No, there isn’t, you can’t get caught up in their lies.” “But,” “I know it’s hard for you, but I have evidence. She carefully placed a newspaper in front of Ruby. A news reporter went missing. “What does this have to do with my parents?” “The news reporter went missing the day after a mass of murders were found. Wolves, millions dead.” Ruby clenched the tablecloth. “How do you know it was my parents?” “The news reporter; my close friend, made a case against your parents. It was strong, strong enough to sentence them to years in jail. He was going to turn it in, but he disappeared. You don’t need to believe me, but now you at least know the truth.” Grandma got up and left, leaving Ruby in stunned silence. She didn’t move for a very long time. The tick of the clock was almost inaudible against her swirling thoughts. A knock on the door severed the silence. Her parents barged in and embraced her. It felt rehearsed, like they had practiced until it was perfect. Usually Ruby would hug them tightly, letting all her emotions flow out until she felt safe again. But she didn’t, she couldn’t let herself choose so quickly. If fate is already written for us, then why do we have to choose?

Ruby stumbled into her grandma's house. The familiar scent wafted through the air. She stifled a sob as she inspected the house. A small table, covered with a dirty table cloth sat in the middle of the room. Ruby hesitantly took a seat. She clasped her hands in her lap. Heart beating wildly against her chest like it wanted to fly out. That would be easier, if I could just not have these feelings. If I didn’t feel these emotions. But then again, if I didn’t then what would the world have become? Am I a monster for wanting to hide away? I could’ve denied it, I could deny it. Then why am I still here?

“Are you okay?” Lupo playfully nudged Ruby. “I mean, I found out my family are killers and raised me to think they were heroes. Then a wolf convinced me they were wrong and brought me to my grandma who my parents forbid me from visiting. So yeah, everything’s fine.” She got up and stormed off. Lupo flattened his ears. “I was just trying to help.” Ruby ran into the guest room and plonked down onto the bed. She curled up and sobbed, tears streaming down her cheeks. She grabbed a nearby teddy bear and clutched it with her trembling hands. She shook violently, her sobs reduced to whimpers.

 “Hey, it’s grandma” Ruby reluctantly turned to face her grandma standing in the doorway. Her face was illuminated with the moonlight that shined in from the window. “What do you think?” Ruby asked, turning back to face the wall. “You used to be so sweet, you would talk to me about everything.” Grandma turned to face the door. “How did your parents change you so much?” Grandma sighed. 

Ruby felt tears forming in her eyes once again. “I’m scared.” She admitted. “I don’t want to share my life because…I’m scared that I’ll be left alone. After that day you told me the truth, I asked them about it and…they left me out in the woods for a night, threatening to leave me there forever. So I played the obedient daughter, listened to their lies until it felt…natural.” Grandma's hand tightened on the door frame. “It’s horrible what your parents have become. Sometimes I wonder; could I have changed it? Is it my fault they’re like this? Maybe it’s not their fault…maybe it’s mine.” 

Ruby abruptly sat up. “No! Grandma, you shouldn’t think like that! The only reason I’m here right now is because you helped me remember my worth. When I felt like no one else did.” Grandma stared deep into Ruby’s dark, grey eyes. “Thank you, I knew there was still a part of you that wasn’t tainted by their lies.” Grandma said, walking off. Ruby smiled; caring and warm, a feeling like someone loved her. A feeling she hadn’t felt for years.

The morning light shone through the window. Ruby slowly opened her wary eyes and gazed up at the white ceiling. She sighed, knowing she’d have to face her parents soon enough. They were like a forgotten memory of a moment. A moment that you never wanted to go back to. A memory of the grief and guilt you felt that you ignored at day and lived in at night. Ruby slowly got up and walked towards the kitchen. There, grandma was washing dishes and Lupo was sitting and watching. He was sprawled across a fluffy dog bed. Ruby sighed as she saw their eyes light up as she walked past. “How are you feeling today?” Lupo's comforting voice made the pain hurt even worse. “Better.” Ruby dryly stated. “I know it’s hard. And we can’t do anything to change that. But just know we’re here if you need us.” Grandma chimed in. “I don’t want your sympathy. Just leave me alone.” Ruby said, anger rising.

A knock shattered the tension. Grandma slowly walked to the window. She drew a sharp breath and turned to face Ruby. Ruby could see the pity in her eyes and knew exactly who was there. “Let them in.” She choked on the last word. Her parents briskly strode in. Their hands still lingered by their sides. Where the knives are. Ruby's face stayed neutral as she stepped closer.  “Mother, father.” She maintained a cold glare. “Little Red Riding Hood.” Her mother replied coolly. I haven’t heard anyone call me that in so long. “We haven’t seen you in so long! We were scared you might have…” She trailed off and started to sob. Fake crying. So original. Ruby maintained her composure as she stepped back into the house. “I know what you’re doing so stop acting like I’m five again.” Ruby's mother abruptly stopped and stared at Ruby pitifully. Ruby’s father stared blankly but as Ruby spoke his gaze shifted. He opened and closed his mouth, finally he spoke up. “Elise, remember…” he whispered. “Of course I remember!” She whispered back angrily. Ruby watched all of this with a composed expression, though all she wanted to do was hide and rid of her problems. “This conversation is getting a bit…out of hand, should we take it inside?”Ruby’s parents looked stunned at the question, but quickly nodded and returned to the facade. Ruby smiled softly and gestured for them to come in. 

Ruby’s parents swiftly walked in and positioned themselves next to the table. “Sit down.” Grandma said in a shaky but certain voice. Ruby neared the shuffling of paws against the wooden floor and quickly excused herself. She briskly walked to the hallway and disappeared behind a corner where Lupo sat, shaking vigorously. “It’s been so long since I’ve seen them…” Lupo whimpered. “I know they can’t kill me here but I panicked and…” His desperate eyes searched Ruby’s as she stroked his fur. “It's okay, you hide for now and I’ll sort things out.” Lupo nodded quickly. Ruby smiled and returned to the dining room. “Okay, so where were we? Oh right, we’ve been so worried about you! We know that when you become a teen you start to grow away, but we didn’t think that it would be this… severe.” Elise said. How are they so convincing? No, they are lying, I can’t let myself forget that. Ruby felt her muscles stiffen and her lungs struggle to take in air. Her parents' lips curled into a small smile. They know I’m too weak, they know they can break me. But I can’t let them win.

 Ruby nodded briefly. She considered retorting but decided it was too soon. Her heart was beating in her chest so loud she was sure her parents would be able to hear it. But if they did, they hid it well. “Remember those days where we would sit together, enjoying life. You were happy—we were happy. Now we take all of that for granted. We are your family, as hard as it is to hear. It’s wrong to abandon those who have been with you this whole time.” Elise continued. “We’ve been here through all of your hard times, and you just left. That’s what happens when you fill your head with lies.” Ruby lowered her gaze. “I-I didn’t leave because I wanted to,” she spoke softly. “I left because I needed time to think. I now realise that it was wrong—I shouldn’t have run away. I should have faced my fears, but I was scared.” Ruby slowly glanced back up at her parents. “I didn’t want to lose you, I never meant for it to happen this way.” Her parents' faces softened slightly. Good. “Honey, it’s okay. You don’t need to cry over it, come with us and we can start again.” Start again. Ruby thought hesitantly. Like all the blood would just…disappear. “That seems…” Ruby measured her options. “Almost too good to be true.”

Lupo lay pressed against the wall, each sharp breath a reminder of reality. She’s lying. She has to be. She couldn’t leave us now…could she? The way she spoke was perfect—too perfect. His stomach twisted as he thought of her leaving. Surely I know her well enough, or maybe she has always been lying. Lupo shuffled just enough to see, and Ruby’s parents' heads snapped to face him. 

“Well, we sure didn’t think we’d see a wolf here.” Elise stood up, fingers tapping the table. “Grandma, what is this?” Ruby said worriedly. Lupo froze. “I think we can use this wolf to our advantage.” Elise stepped forward and her smile grew; thin and cold. She turned to face Ruby. “Little red riding hood, in order to prove your loyalty. Kill this wolf.” 

No. Lupo thought, doubt creeping in. Grandma watched warily as Elise grabbed a knife from the kitchen and handed it to Ruby. She held it in her trembling hands. “O-okay, I’ll do it.” Ruby said, mind racing. She slowly stepped towards Lupo, knife in hand. Lupo whimpered as he looked back at Ruby with pleading eyes. Please, no. She pressed the knife against Lupo's throat and he tensed—muscles stiffening. She pressed harder until the blade drew blood, then hesitated; fear creeping in. Ruby gazed into Lupo's desperate eyes as he winced. Ruby’s grip on the knife tightened and she cut across his neck. Blood spilled out as Lupo fell into a heap on the floor, trembling. His body went limp and cold and Ruby stepped back, stunned. “I did it. Do you trust me now?” She choked on the words. “Well done, now shall we go home?” Elise turned and walked out with Ruby’s father trailing closely behind her, not waiting for an answer. Grandma stared at Ruby with an unreadable expression. Not hate, not fear, but pity. Ruby followed her parents solemnly but obediently. She slipped the knife into her pocket and did not glance back at the blood stained floor. Lupo's corpse lay still and lifeless as grandma rushed over to him.

Grandma heard the slam of the door and turned to face the hallway, walking through the empty rooms. Too stunned to cry she walked into Ruby’s room and sat down on the bed. Then she saw something, a glint of light reflecting off an object. She stepped closer and found a small vial. A potion. Grandma smiled. “I knew she wouldn’t have.” She whispered, and turned to run back to Lupo.

(One month later)
Ruby sat alone in her small room, staring longingly out the window. Then she saw it—a ruffle of grey fur, partially stained crimson among the leafy forest. I knew grandma would find it. Ruby smiled and her fingers gently brushed the hilt of the knife that laid on her desk. Maybe I’ve become what I’ve always feared. I never wanted to be like my parents, but maybe learning from them was partially good. Their manipulation is their own downfall. She stuffed the knife into her pocket and walked up to her door. She paused with her hand on the doorknob. If the wolf dies and no one’s around, I’ll be the one to tell the story.

The end

creations.write_up:
Fractured Reflection
My vision blurred open to see the red flashing numbers on my clock. I got up as usual, went to school, slept, and repeated. But today felt different. Nothing felt right. Everyone around me looked… weird, uncanny, the eldritch city was collapsing before my very eyes.
I slumped in my chair, the lecture hall felt eerie, and every word my teacher
said was muffled by my own thoughts. Why did I feel so on edge? Why did I
feel so misplaced in the puzzle piece of life?
The bell screeched.
The sound snapping me out of my thoughts. I walked through the halls, my lethargy weighing me down. As I exited, the crisp evening air bit at my face and I put my self-heating jacket on and walked towards the teleportation
platform to my street.
“June!” Annie exclaims with urgency.
“Hey Annie, what is-” Annie cuts me off before I can finish my sentence. She
holds a mirror up to my face.
“Look.” She says sharply.
I looked at my reflection, but I didn’t look like me; I looked like everyone I
walked past on the street. The last time I saw myself in the mirror was in New
York, before I woke up stuck here, along with everyone else.
I knew mirrors were forbidden; the government couldn’t let the truth seep out of this “perfect city” they had so evilly curated. Now I knew why. The secrets are enveloped in our very own streets, and yet we still walk along them oblivious.
But I knew.

I knew that they would take us, brainwash us, clone us, as we would supposedly become the “superior versions of ourselves”. I couldn’t stay here a minute longer.
“Annie, we need to get out of here!” I dragged her to the poster on the wall
about the new super-speed trains.
“This is our one-way ticket back to New York!”
The city lights shone as we arrived at the ticket booth of the train station, and a woman sat behind the thin glass, looking unimpressed.
“Hi,” I squint my eyes, trying to read her name. She looked me up and down,
then rolled her eyes.
“It’s Jenny.” She spat the words out coldly.
“Two tickets to New York, please.”
Her nails clacked on the keyboard. “No can do, there’s no availability.”
A huge electric pink bubble of gum popped in our faces, then she shooed us away.
We rushed onto the platform. The bright screen read 9 pm train to New York departing in 1 minute. The train slammed to a halt, the brakes squeaking, the bright blue doors hissing open. Passengers rushed on a whirlwind of chatter and madness surrounded us. We blended in with the crowd, cautious not to get caught. The doors slammed behind me.
“We made it, Annie-”.
But Annie wasn’t there; she wasn’t anywhere. I frantically looked out the
window, only to see Annie being pulled away by two metallic policemen.
“Annie!” I yelled, but she couldn’t hear me.
I watched them drag her weak body to the cells. I tried to get off the train, but I was stuck. Trapped between hundreds of people squashed together. Guilt punched my body. It was too late; I couldn’t save her now.
I arrived in New York; a white film blurred around me. I was normal, I was me again, I wasn’t a government experiment part of that horrid clone city… I had escaped!
Then, suddenly, my vision went dark.
I couldn’t think straight.
My legs felt like jelly, and my body felt weak. My eyes shut, and I slowly collapsed before waking up in a dark cell. I looked around, a teal, indestructible barrier blocking the only exit.
Where was I? An intense feeling of déjà vu washed over me.
I had been here before.
A loud robotic voice filtered through the intercom.
“No one escapes and gets away with it. Not even you.”

creations.write_up:
Not alone

It towered over me,
But I wasn’t scared. 
It was bigger than me, 
But I didn’t run. 
It screamed,
But I whispered. 
It was scary, 
But I was not. 
It was angry,
But I was calm. 
I reached out to hold its hand,
But it threw me off. 
I gasped,
But it laughed at me. 
This made me more determined to befriend it. 
I placed my hand back towards it,
And it grunted loudly. 
I looked into its eyes,
But it looked the other way.
I tapped it on the shoulder,
To remind it I was still looking at it. 
This time,
It locked eyes with me. 
And it was at that moment that I realised,
That it was scared. 
I realised in that second,
That whoever it was, whoever you are,
And whatever it is, and whatever you look like,
It, you, we will be living,
You and I, just alike.

creations.write_up:
The tiger, the bird and the river
She was sitting down next to the lake and was staring at the fish. Tabbi was calm. Her daily routine always starts like this. Next, she will get up and catch her breakfast, a rabbit. After she eats it, she will eventually go back to staring at the beautiful Chinese rivers. She loved the sound of flowing water, it's her favourite sound! A bird flew by. Flap, flap! Tabbi was swatting her paw at the koi. She did this for fun. After, she caught lunch. A delicious fish. The bird was sitting. She swatted at the koi and... BANG! She fell in the water! Bird knew danger was coming. What would Tabbi do? Bird called his friends and they pulled her out. Finally! She thanked Bird and his friends for getting her out. They had a big party with their favourite foods. The end 🐅🐦

This is Jery, and a little story about him.
One day a pizza called Jery was made. All Jery knew was that he was bound for great things. Jery was confused when they put him in a box with lots of other pieces of pizza.
Jery thought it was a way to go out in the world and take him to his destiny. Although it wasn’t a glorious ride when he arrived somewhere. The man who took us there gave a man in the house the box of pizza. When the stranger in the house opened the box he ate one of the pizza slices! I was shocked, I escaped and lived. 
I decided to become a dancer and lived happily ever after.

creations.write_up:
This is the story about my character I designed with Polymer clay and he is so far my very best magical creature. 

The Curious Adventures of Mr Blinky Tickletoes 🐸🍄

Deep in a leafy corner of the garden lived a peculiar little fellow named Mr Blinky Tickletoes. No one was quite sure what kind of creature he was. Some said he was part goblin, part potato, and part mushroom patch.

Mr Blinky had moss growing on his back (which he refused to comb because he said it was “fashionable”) and two tiny mushrooms that popped up whenever he laughed too hard.

His best friend was a small green frog named Sir Squibbles, who he carried everywhere like a precious treasure. Sir Squibbles didn’t talk much, but he was an excellent listener and gave very wise blinks.

Every morning Mr Blinky would wobble out of his mossy nook and declare,
“Another perfect day for extremely important nonsense!”

Sometimes they went on grand adventures like searching for the world’s slipperiest leaf, or trying to convince snails to join a marching band.

Once, during a particularly enthusiastic giggle, one of Mr Blinky’s mushrooms popped off and bounced down the path. Sir Squibbles simply blinked twice and hopped after it.

“See?” said Mr Blinky proudly. “This is why every great explorer needs a frog.”

And so the two friends continued their curious life… wandering the garden, collecting odd things, and laughing so much that the mushrooms on Mr Blinky’s back kept growing bigger and bigger.

Which was quite convenient.

Because they made excellent hats for frogs.

creations.write_up: Looming in the shadows of spooky street is a house. It's right next to a grave yard, all the houses next door are for sale. Lily Packer from across the street got a dare to enter. She walked to the gate, creek it went, and she opened it cautiously. It almost felt more chilly in the property than just by the gate. The door was left unlocked. Lily went through the hall where there were portraits of people and some of cats, Lily had never seen them at the shops or at park runs. There was music coming from upstairs. “Maybe there's a party," thought Lily. The next room was spine chilling, there was a big pot full of some substance, it was bubbling and really stunk, bleh. The music got louder as she climbed the ladder up. Above the ladder was a room with a piano and music, yet no people or anything. The seat for the piano was velvet and leather. The room had cobwebs on the window. This was horrific. There were some stairs up to the attic. Up in the attic was something worse than anything she had seen. AHHHHHHHHH. That's the last anyone had ever heard of Lily.

creations.write_up: In year 3, we learned about semi abstract art. Moira Hazel was our inspiration for this artwork. We started with shapes for the landscape. Then we used different textured materials (bubblewrap, fork...) with paint to colour the shapes. We had to choose one main australian native flora and two other plants. The main one had to be more prominent. I'm really proud of my artwork.

creations.write_up:
Why you should love Guinea pigs:

My name is Hannah and I’m a big guinea pig fan, and you should be too! Guinea pigs have to be the cutest, funnest pet (my guinea pigs, Chocolate and Truffle, totally agree). There a lots of different breeds and there has to be one for you! 

Guinea pigs are such great pets because they can teach responsibility, help you feel better when you’re sad, and most importantly, they are so much fun!

In conclusion, I think that you should love guinea pigs because they are the cutest, cuddliest pals ever!!! Bye!
